the-mad-podcast-with-matt-turck.name: The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
the-mad-podcast-with-matt-turck.bio: Podcast: How to Build Long-Horizon AI Agents — Mitch Troyanovsky, Basis

html_en:
Two stories dominate today's AI conversation: the maturation of the agentic layer — with new lessons on building agents that actually work in production — and a wave of platform integrations that quietly reshape how developers build on top of AI.

The Agent Realist's Guide

Everyone is building agents. Far fewer are building agents that work. This episode of the MAD Podcast with Matt Turck featuring Mitch Troyanovsky, cofounder of Basis — a unicorn building AI agents that complete entire tax returns end-to-end, autonomously, over hours or days — is the most practically useful thing you'll read this week on the subject.

Troyanovsky's framing of agents is refreshingly grounded. On the challenge of non-determinism:

"Humans are already used to working with non-deterministic systems, it's just the systems are normally their co-workers, not their computers. And in many ways, companies and processes is all about how do you design a system for non-deterministic entities to coordinate together to solve a problem? And once you realize that, it's kind of like agent design."

On the limits of evals — a point that will sting anyone who's ever felt smug about a green test suite:

"Let's say you have 100 evals. Great. They all pass. Are you confident that now generalizes to the real world, to production? And our answer has been no. Even if you got it right 100 out of 100 times, if a person is just getting it right because they're going to Wikipedia, the accounting firm wouldn't hire them, and so they shouldn't hire us either."

Perhaps the most counterintuitive insight: the team at Basis literally whispers into microphones all day — not as an affectation, but as a productivity technique. The reasoning is elegant:

"Speaking is just so much faster than writing things down, and in fact when you try to write things down you are essentially trying to summarize all the crazy thoughts in your head. To an agent, they don't care — they would actually prefer the raw stream. So it becomes much more productive to be able to whisper your thoughts."

And perhaps the sharpest heuristic for anyone building context-heavy AI systems:

"You'll see people freaking out over a code file that isn't abstracted properly, and yet their context is total shit. The English is more precious because the English affects the performance. The code does not affect the performance."

Platform Integrations: The Quiet Power Move

Two significant developer integrations dropped today that deserve more attention than they're getting.

First, Anthropic announced Foundation Models framework support for Claude via a new Swift package. Apple developers can now use Apple's on-device models for lightweight tasks — summarization, extraction, journaling prompts — and seamlessly hand off to Claude when the request demands multi-step reasoning, web search, or code execution. The result is a single user experience backed by the right model at each step. The package handles streaming, tool calls, and structured responses back into SwiftUI views. It works on iOS 27, macOS 27, and the rest of Apple's upcoming platform stack.

Garry Tan captured a related sentiment about the new power available to developers in agentic workflows:

"The most surprising thing about using GStack pre-Fable 5 and after is now for many one-way-door questions you might get back in Claude Code, you can actually just say 'Take all recommendations' and be happy."

Second, Josh Woodward announced that Gemini 2.5 Flash has arrived in the Gemini App — a notable speed-and-cost play from Google as the model wars continue. Meanwhile, Google Labs highlighted Pomelli (AI product photography → video/GIFs for small businesses) and Flow (visual storytelling) as its Labs experiments gaining real traction.

The Cursor Playbook, Annotated

Cursor's reported valuation continues to generate commentary, and Box CEO Aaron Levie wrote what is arguably the best post-mortem on why it worked — and what it means for every applied AI builder:

"Most people completely underestimated the market size in AI coding. The biggest developer tool exits in history were on the order of low billions of dollars... Multiple mental models shattered near instantly. Cursor provided out the applied AI playbook by figuring out the right product shape for agentic coding work, acting as a neutral layer between models and the workflows, post-training models for the areas that make most sense to drive down costs or improve performance, building out the right infra stack for the relevant workflows, building out a strong category-aligned GTM motion, and more."

@realmadhuguru added the Jevons Paradox framing that makes this durable rather than a one-off:

"Making steam engines more efficient increased coal demand. Higher-level languages made programming easier and resulted in far more software being built... When the cost and complexity of a task falls, new use cases become economically viable. AI + software engineering will likely follow the same pattern."

The Changing Shape of a Workday

Matt Turck captured something true in a deceptively simple diagram:

Before AI: [decision] [process] [process] [decision] [process] [process] [process] — 10pm: still going.
With AI: [decision] [decision] [decision] [decision] [decision] — 3pm: [brain empty] [need coffee] [staring at wall]

The joke lands because it's real. AI collapses the processing overhead and concentrates cognitive work into decisions. What nobody quite knows yet is whether humans are built to sustain that density — or whether we need the filler to recover. @swyx had a related observation about Databricks' $188B fundraise: "The M in their Series M stands for 'we are going to kill so many meetings.'" The subtext being that meetings, annoying as they are, have historically been where humans process, align, and recover. Eliminating them entirely may surface new costs we haven't accounted for yet.

Worth Watching

Watch/Listen: How to Build Long-Horizon AI Agents — Mitch Troyanovsky, Basis (MAD Podcast) — genuinely one of the better technical conversations on agent design in recent months. Don't skim it.

Thomas Sottiaux of OpenAI is crowd-sourcing Codex use cases — "What's a hard problem Codex solved for you this week? Where do you learn from others on how to push the frontier?" — worth following the replies if you're exploring what frontier usage actually looks like. And Peter Yang's teardown of X's open-source spam detection algorithm is a useful reminder that behavioral modeling without content analysis leaves a very exploitable gap — one that sophisticated AI content mills are almost certainly already using.
html_zh:
AI基础设施的投资狂潮与产品创新齐头并进，Cursor的成功正在重塑整个行业对"applied AI"的理解——而真正的护城河，从来不是模型本身。

🏗️ Cursor效应：applied AI的教科书级示范

本周最热议的话题之一，是Cursor估值暴涨背后的产品逻辑。Aaron Levie 在推文中给出了迄今最清晰的复盘：

"Cursor提供了applied AI的完整剧本：找到正确的产品形态，成为模型与工作流之间的中立层，在关键环节做后训练以降低成本或提升性能，搭建匹配的基础设施，建立强大的品类GTM动作。我们还会看到更多这样的案例。"
— @levie

@realmadhuguru 则从更宏观的历史视角呼应了这一判断：蒸汽机效率提升带来更多煤炭需求，高级编程语言让软件数量爆炸，电子表格让财务分析无处不在——AI与软件工程的结合，很可能遵循同样的模式，让以前"经济上不可行"的问题也找到解法。

"当所有人都能用AI构建产品，你的差异化就变成了：产品感知、领域知识、分发能力和执行力。"
— @realmadhuguru

🤖 长周期AI Agent：会计是最硬的试炼场

Watch/Listen: How to Build Long-Horizon AI Agents — Mitch Troyanovsky, Basis | The MAD Podcast

本期MAD Podcast堪称近期最值得细听的AI工程实践对话。Basis联合创始人Mitch Troyanovsky深入拆解了如何构建能自主运行数小时乃至数天的Agent系统——他们的目标是让AI端到端完成整张税单。

Mitch有一个振聋发聩的洞察：大多数人高估了eval的意义。

"假设你有100个eval，全部通过，看起来很好。但你有信心它能泛化到真实生产环境吗？我们的答案是：没有。即使100次全对，如果一个人只是靠查Wikipedia得出答案，会计事务所不会雇用他们，所以也不应该雇用我们。"

他们还有一个在办公室引发好奇的习惯——对着麦克风低声说话。原因很简单：

"给AI上下文，说话比打字快太多了。你把脑子里所有乱七八糟的想法直接说出来，AI不会嫌烦——事实上它更喜欢这样。Agent设计的核心，其实就是为非确定性实体设计协作系统——这和管理一家公司没有本质区别。"

另一个犀利观点：工程师往往过度关注代码抽象，却忽视了最关键的东西。

"你会看到有人为代码文件的抽象不规范而抓狂，但他们的上下文说明写得一团糟。英文（提示词）更珍贵，因为它直接影响性能；代码不影响性能。"

📱 Google与Anthropic的平台卡位战

产品层面，两家公司都在悄悄扩大阵地。Google方面，Josh Woodward 宣布 Gemini 2.5 Flash已上线Gemini App，同时Google Labs旗下面向小微企业的营销工具 Pomelli 新增了将产品图转化为短视频或GIF的功能。

Anthropic则出手更具战略意味：官方博客宣布，Claude将通过全新Swift Package接入Apple的Foundation Models框架，让iOS/macOS开发者可以在本地模型处理简单任务（摘要、提取）后，无缝将复杂推理、代码生成、网络搜索等任务交由Claude完成——对用户而言是一体验，背后是"最合适的模型做最合适的事"。

与此同时，Guillermo Rauch 宣称Vercel已成为"全球最快的AI Gateway基础设施"，基础设施层的竞争分毫不让。

🛡️ X平台的AI内容困境

Peter Yang 深入研究了X的开源算法，发现其反AI垃圾内容机制存在明显盲区：

"这个行为模型叫TweetSpamBot，分析账号最近512条操作，识别TWEET_CREATE_BURST、QUOTE_TWEET_SPAMMER等模式。问题在于，模型根本不读帖子的实际内容。一个精明的AI内容工厂完全可以每天持续发垃圾内容：找到热门帖子→用同一模板引用（hook→数字→故事→结论）→每天10次以上重复。如果X不想变成另一个LinkedIn，就应该重点关注这类账号。"
— @petergyang

💡 今日金句

Matt Turck 用一张幽默的"工作日演化图"道尽了AI时代知识工作者的新处境：

"AI之前：[决策][流程][流程][决策][流程][流程][流程]，晚上10点还没完。
有了AI：[决策][决策][决策][决策][决策]，下午3点：[大脑空白][需要咖啡][盯着墙发呆]"
— @mattturck

Databricks的$188B融资也被 @swyx 一语道破：这轮融资的"M"代表"我们将消灭无数会议"（we are going to kill so many meetings）。资本正在用真金白银投票，押注的不是AI能做什么，而是AI能省掉什么。
